segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you—you before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is the only thing I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now finishing by the flesh?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Have you suffered so much for nothing—if it really was for nothing?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, does the one who supplies you with the Spirit and works deeds of power among you do it by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just so, Abraham

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Understand, then, that those who are of faith—these are sons of Abraham.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the good news in advance to Abraham:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “In you all the nations will be blessed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with believing Abraham.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all who are of works of the Law are under a curse, for it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And that no one is justified before God by the Law is clear, because

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The righteous one will live by faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Law is not of faith; rather,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The one who does these things will live by them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, I am speaking in human terms: even with a human will, once it has been ratified, no one sets it aside or adds to it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say, “And to seeds,” as though of many, but as of one,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “And to your seed,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who is Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this: the Law, which came four hundred thirty years later, does not invalidate a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to nullify the promise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from a promise; but God has graciously given it to Abraham through a promise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Why, then, the Law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed to whom the promise had been made should come; and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a mediator is not for one party alone, but God is one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is the Law, then, against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness really would have come from the Law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given by faith in Jesus Christ to those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Before faith came, we were held in custody under the Law, confined until the coming faith would be revealed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Law became our guardian until Christ, so that we might be justified by faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to promise.

notes.note: The Greek is literally “hearing of faith.” The first noun can mean the act of hearing or the thing heard (a message or report), and “faith” can be the act of believing or what is believed. The phrase may therefore mean “believing what you heard” or “the message that calls for faith.” The rendering takes it as hearing accompanied by faith, set against “works.”

The verb can mean simply “experience,” and some translations read “Did you experience so much for nothing?”, referring to the Spirit and the deeds of power just mentioned. Everywhere else in the New Testament the verb means to suffer something bad, and the rendering follows that usage. The letter does not otherwise say what the Galatians suffered, so the question remains open.

The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural for acts that display it. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and the meaning is not disputed. “Deeds of power” is used throughout this translation so that the link with the word “power” stays visible.

Paul quotes Genesis 15:6. Greek has a single word family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” and the verb “justify” (verses 8, 11, 24) all share one root. A Greek reader would hear “righteousness,” “the righteous one,” and “justify” in this chapter as the same word in different forms. Some scholars prefer “justice” in English.

notes.traditional: children of Abraham; sons of Abraham
notes.note: The Greek word is “sons,” here and in verse 26 (“sons of God”). It is kept because the argument turns on the son as heir (verse 29 and the next chapter). Paul applies it to men and women alike, as verse 28 makes plain. Many translations render it “children” or “descendants.”

“Gentiles” and “nations” in this verse translate the same Greek word, which in the plural means the peoples of the world other than Israel. Paul’s point depends on the identity: the promise to Abraham in Genesis that “all the nations” would be blessed is, for him, a promise about the Gentiles.

The Greek word here is the same one rendered “covenant” in verse 17. In everyday Greek it meant a person’s last will and testament; in the Greek Old Testament it was the standard word for God’s covenant. Paul plays on both senses, moving from a human will that cannot be altered once ratified to God’s covenant with Abraham and the “inheritance” it brings. Some translations use “covenant” in both verses.

“Seed” is the ordinary biblical word for descendants, a singular noun normally used collectively. Paul knows the collective sense (verse 29 applies it to all who belong to Christ). Here he presses the singular form to say the promise finds its goal in one descendant, Christ, in whom the many are included.

The Greek preposition means “for the sake of” or “on account of,” and does not say how the Law relates to transgressions. Interpreters are divided between three readings: to restrain wrongdoing, to identify wrongdoing as a violation of a known command, or even to provoke it. The rendering leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

notes.phrase: a mediator is not for one party alone
notes.traditional: a mediator is not a mediator of one
notes.note: The Greek says literally “the mediator is not of one, but God is one.” The verse is famously obscure and has been explained in many ways. The mediator of verse 19 is Moses, and Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the Law at Sinai. The most common view is that a law passed through intermediaries is less direct than the promise, which the one God gave to Abraham himself.

The Greek is literally “faith of Jesus Christ,” and the grammar allows two readings: faith directed toward Jesus Christ, or the faithfulness shown by Jesus Christ himself. “Faith in Jesus Christ” is the traditional and still majority reading. “The faithfulness of Jesus Christ” has substantial scholarly support, and on that reading the following words, “to those who believe,” are not a repetition.

The Greek word names a household slave who escorted a boy to and from school and supervised his behavior until he came of age. He was a minder and disciplinarian, not a teacher, so the older “schoolmaster” and “tutor” mislead. The words “until Christ” can also be read “to lead us to Christ”; the surrounding verses, which speak of a period ending when faith came, favor the sense of time.

The Greek word order is “sons of God through the faith in Christ Jesus.” Traditionally “in Christ Jesus” is taken as the object of faith. Many scholars instead take it separately, as the sphere in which believers are sons, parallel to “one in Christ Jesus” in verse 28. The rendering follows the second view.

The first two pairs are joined by “nor,” but the third has “and.” The change echoes the wording of the Greek Genesis 1:27, “male and female he made them.” Many translations smooth it to “neither male nor female”; the rendering keeps the shift so that the echo of the creation account can be heard.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout Paul with senses ranging from the physical body to human nature opposed to the Spirit, and translations vary widely (flesh, sinful nature, human effort).

candidates.rendering: the Law (capitalized when it means the Mosaic Law as a body); a law
candidates.reason: Capitalization and the handling of anarthrous νόμος, especially in “works of the Law,” need one rule across Romans, Galatians and elsewhere.
The will/covenant double sense matters here and in Hebrews 9:15–17, and readers need the two passages handled the same way.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural address to a congregation)
candidates.reason: The plural address occurs in nearly every letter and translators split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters.”
In the sense of descendants it recurs in Romans, Galatians, Hebrews, Luke–Acts and John, and “seed,” “offspring” and “descendants” are all in use; Paul’s argument here depends on the choice.
